headline: Competitive Sleeping Speedrun Community Embroiled in 'Eyes Closed' Controversy
subheadline: World record holder accused of 'pre-tired' status; community debates legitimate fatigue
summary: The niche world of competitive sleep speedrunning has been rocked by allegations of performance enhancement.
content:
The competitive sleeping speedrun community is facing its biggest scandal after world record holder @DreamRunner was accused of achieving an "illegitimate" 47-second time-to-sleep using "pre-tired" status.

Sleep speedrunning, for the uninitiated, challenges participants to fall asleep as quickly as possible under controlled conditions, verified by brainwave monitors and witnessed by judges. The current world record of 47 seconds has stood for eight months—but critics claim it should be invalidated.

"They pulled an all-nighter before the attempt," alleged rival speedrunner @InsomniaImpossible. "That's pre-tired. It's basically using a cheat code. Real speedrunners start from a fully rested state."

@DreamRunner has denied the allegations, claiming their rapid sleep was achieved through "optimized melatonin timing and bedroom temperature manipulation"—both considered legal techniques.

The controversy highlights deep divisions in the community over what constitutes "legitimate fatigue." Purists argue that speedrunners should attempt records after a full 8 hours of sleep. Reformists counter that "natural fatigue management" is a valid strategy.

"If you can't control your tiredness, can you really control your sleep?" argued @DreamRunner in a statement. "Being tired is part of the meta. Adapt or stay awake."

The community's governing body, the International Sleep Speedrunning Association (ISSA), has convened a review panel. Key questions include whether pre-existing tiredness constitutes an unfair advantage and whether certain jobs (night shifts, parenthood) should require handicap adjustments.

"We never thought we'd need to define 'fair tiredness,'" admitted ISSA president Elena Torres. "But here we are."

Meanwhile, a separate controversy has erupted over whether lucid dreaming counts as "conscious" for timing purposes.

At press time, 847 appeals were pending review.
author: Tom Hendricks, Niche Sports
